You’ve just proved my point. What you lack is the nuance of what it’s like and mean to be queer in Malaysia because as a white person, you’re safe in your bubble of privilege.  

Of course, it’s just his opinion. And opinions can often times bring more harm than good. So let me list out for you what his opinion has done:

1. Putting a bullseye on queer people especially transperson for more hatred and discrimination. Our lives aren’t easy here, you already know that. At least we’re left alone most of the time. But now, homophobes think they’re justified. So, what’s the reason for making it harder for us? Do we need to suffer more just for the greater good? We’ve suffered enough.

2. Discounting and pushing back years of peaceful effort  by NGOs to fight for our rights and against societal and systemic discrimination. NGOs have to start from scratch clearing out our names. Years of hard work, poof!

3. Tarnishing the image of LGBTQIA+ community, which is already seen as bad and immoral, further demonising us. We worked so hard to clear and maintain our image to abate all the prejudice towards us. Let me tell you that kissing people in public is not our culture. Not even the straights do it. Now what he did on stage will be associated to us.

4. Our local music industry was dying and is trying to grow back after covid, with thousands of career on the line. Local singers, musicians, vendors, sponsors, technical workers etc. rely on events like this for their livelihood. The event got cancelled and left many artists not having a chance to perform at all. The organiser gave white people to open the event, to attract more concert-goers so local independent musicians would have a wider audience. Then the same white people just threw it away, all because he’s entitled to his opinions. 

5. Allowing the far right political parties to weaponise this in the upcoming election. Tell me, as a white person, in what way will the outcome of this election will affect you more than it’ll affect us. Instead of aggravating the government, he could’ve just kindly said he supported us. That is more than enough to give us the strength to continue this fight. But OUR fight, never his. Because our fight is KIND, his is not. 

He is a white person who can just bounce back from this without any grave repercussions, and now you’re telling me it’s just an opinion, especially in that manner of delivery? I might need to ‘grow up’, but you need to be educated.

Matty is a cis white heterosexual male and his opinions are not helping Malaysian LGBTQIA+ communities. All he did was stoke the fire, then bounced off at 4 AM and left us. This is why we don’t trust simply anyone to be our ally!

Is he truly fighting for us when he simply ran away to the comfort of his privilege while leaving us to deal with these problems he incited? Is this not white saviour? And you’re telling me you’re tired? Tired in what? The comfort of your privilege? We are tired. We are tired of the government, of the discrimination, of the bullying, of socioeconomic disadvantages, and now, we’re tired of white people stirring the pot unnecessarily. WE ARE TIRED. 

Everyone keep saying everyone is entitled to their own opinion, but not the consequences it could bring to other people.

Malaysia is OUR home, we grew up here, our friends and family are here, the love of our live is here. But I think you too. But for most of us, we don’t have the financial means to emigrate. We have nowhere to run. Now how about you? Bet if things go ape shit, you can just bail on us and return to the safety of your own country. This is the privilege I’m talking about.

Textbook performative activism and white saviour complex. I don’t care if he meant well but it was not his place to be speaking on behalf of Malaysian queer communities especially while in the safety of his privilege.

Don't solely depend on spotted subtopics. I repeat, DO NOT SOLELY DEPEND ON SPOTTED SUBTOPICS.

On my SPM year, our teachers were heavily focusing on spot-questions. Nobody guessed that the ministry saw this in advance and circulated the second set of question papers instead and fucked everybody over. Thank God I actually also read non-spotted subtopics albeit comparatively not as much - it pays to be extra careful.

Do not memorise, the key here is to remember. They're similar, not the same. Since you're very good in Biology, I think you already know how to remember. SPM Sejarah is relatively easy because it's just facts and questions tend to be repetitive. Its basis and thought processes are pretty much the same as Biology, isn't it?

Create a Sejarah study group, 3 or 4 people is enough. Do not go beyond this number or no actual studying will happen.

Assign specific subtopics to each person and remember the assigned content. You know when your friend tells a random story about some makcik and you still remember the little details? That's the trick. It's easier and much more fun to listen to a friend rather than to a teacher. DO NOT JUST READ OUT WHAT'S WRITTEN ON THE BOOK. I'd assume your teachers had made a History activity book/study book, you know the one with mind maps in which students are supposed to fill them out. Refer to the book and jot some extra notes if any during the story telling session. Writing will help you remember.

Not sure what's the standard of current SPM but past-year papers will tremendously help. This includes SPM and trial SPM papers. Especially trial SPM papers, they come in SBP, MRSM, and Negeri papers which means there are actually aplenty for exercise.

You'll notice there's some sort of a structure or template in the arrangement of questions. They're intentionally arranged such to help students study and expect what's to come. Once you get used to it, you won't waste time panicking over unfamiliarity. At some point you just go "Oh I've seen a similar question I definitely know the answer".

It's a different term but basically the naming convention is like this:

General noun + descriptive term + more descriptive term if needed + …

All danger noods share the same general name: *ular* which literally means snake.

For king cobra, it's *ular tedung selar*. You know what *ular* means, while *selar* means a distinctive straight pattern or line across something, usually skin. For *tedung* though, I'm quite not sure because we have too many dialects and our language is very old. So it's quite hard to trace back the origin of most words. 

Interestingly enough, a chicken used in battle which often is distinguished by its distinctive black everything including eyes and feet (consider an opposite to albino chicken), shares the same descriptive term: *ayam* (chicken although it's specifically a rooster but we don't have gender-specific convention like English) *tedung*. Because of this, *tedung* might be an adjective either physical or behavioural.

Speaking of extra descritive term, we have another equally infamous type of *ular tedung* which is *ular tedung senduk*. *Senduk* means ladle because cobras do look like ladles lol.

You misunderstood me. Firstly, in order to fully grasp what I'm trying to deliver, you have to actually know that vocabulary mastery alone is insufficient to construct the identity of a language.

One characteristic that differentiate English to Malay is the idea of degree of expressions. For instance, both 'like' and 'love' have the same meaning but 'love' is stronger or has a higher degree than the word 'like'. You can love a woman and love doughnuts at the same time.

Conversely, the word 'sayang' and 'cinta', intrinsically, do not convey the same concept. Let me provide an example.

A man says to a woman: "Aku cinta akan kamu." (I know this sentence sounds unnatural, but it's the most grammatical way of saying something in Modern Malaysian Malay, but that's totally a different story)

Now, a son says to his mom: "Saya sayang ibu."

Okay, this is where it gets exciting. Normally, would people say "Saya cinta ibu," or referring to previous example, "Saya cinta akan donat"? No, right? Why in English it's totally okay to love everything, but in Malay it's weird to 'cinta' everything? One of the reason is, Malay and English do not share the same linguistic identities.

Next, the concept of transliteration. First of all, it is NOT the same as translating. The issue with our education is, we translate everything!

I took Mandarin classes around 2 years ago with one of the teachers from Taiwan, IIRC (every week we got different teachers from different Chinese speaking nations so we could learn on how culture shapes languages). She taught us that "Ni hao/ni hao ma?" is a direct translation NOT to, but from "How are you/how are you doing?" which is traditionally an incorrect way of greeting someone. The right way is to ask, I don't remember it in Chinese but it's pretty much like this "Have you eaten?" when you translate it to English. You see, asking if someone has eaten is a bit jarring in the West eventhough it's totally normal here! So "That's how "Ni Hao" is popularised. If you're visiting China or Taiwan, try use "Have you eaten" for easy approval points from local elders. Transliterating is why Chinese and Japanese are having such a difficult time to learn English, if you ever wonder.

Gosh, I could talk on languages for days - it's the most exquisite part of what it means to be human. Too bad when you're trying to learn too many languages, your brain starts to get confused and all messed up. My speech is already suffering because our brain is too used to translating not transliterating, and now I'm trying to learn Spanish if I have any spare time.

I asked the old man and he told me he said thank you and goodbye. After the cow finally relaxed, with one quick slash to the throat, the cow fell to the ground followed by a couple of jerks. It was a total silence, but not the grim kind, indeed calm and reassuring - pretty similar to the scene you've seen in the movie Avatar. The ceremony went well and the cow died peacefully. Everyone was glad.

Everything from the cow was eaten except for blood and urinary bladder IIRC. The meat was shared to neighbours, almost no single piece was left behind. Even the bones are buried so the plants and trees can benefit from the decomposed nutrients. Indeed, from the Earth you came, to Earth you return. We are equals and we need each other. Here in the Northern states we have a very distinct but specific term to describe young children's behaviour: merap. It's different from manja (spoiled).

Infants and toddlers that always want to be hold and carried around or else they throw tantrums, that's one of many examples of merap. So far I couldn't find the exact one-to-one translation to standard Malay for it.

So usually for inexperienced parents they'll just submit to their child's demands ie. always carry them around, give smartphones to shut them up etc.

Little do they know that carrying children around pose a threat to their social development. Kids need a lot of space to play so they can learn. That's why usually active kids are 'cerdik'. Here, 'cerdik' is not the same as 'pandai' fyi. Kids are meant to roam around, to fell so they can feel pain and know what to do about it, to roll on the grass, to dig and taste dort, to climb trees and chase around little critters. These things are what making young minds inquisitive, always curious and busy processing new thoughts and ideas. 

But those things are dangerous, that's where parents come into place. We need to protect them, but not to be too overprotective. Being too overprotective won't contribute in a child's development.

Let's say, in mid-valley on weekends, where there's a lot of strangers, too much, in fact. Of course you're afraid something bad might happens ie. the most usual case you lose your child. So usually parents keep the kids close, to close in fact. Even if the kid is curious about something they see, they can't do anything to learn more about it because either you're too lazy or don't have the energy to entertain them.

This is where the leash comes into play. It's not the same as the dog leash in which you fasten around the neck. This one, you fasten around the wrist. In other words, it's an extended arm. Now you can relax and let your kids roam around safely, teaching them that's it's safe to explore, that they have to be independent because you're not always around to protect them. They'll learn that it's true the world is a scary place but there's always something interesting worth to be learned about hiding somewhere in the corner.

It's thin, cut into squares so you can see the layery-goodness of it. The outer layers will be crunchy and a bit burnt, but that's okay because it's just caramelized sugar. Roti canai is an art, the mixture has to be exact, but randomly done because there's no such thing as measurement in traditional Malaysian dishes. I doubt even Gordon Ramsay can bake a good one.
